newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Reuters 1996 profits climb 17 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Reuters 1996 profits climb 17 pct.

text.p: International news and information group Reuters Holdings Plc on Tuesday reported a 17 percent rise in full-year profits for 1996 and said it still hoped to return surplus cash to shareholders.

Reuters posted 1996 pre-tax profits of 701 million pounds ($1.15 billion) and announced a 20 percent rise in the total dividend to 11.75 pence per share after revenue grew by eight percent to 2.91 billion pounds.
But the company said it would be difficult to improve on its underlying revenue growth rate this year.
Reuters shares were trading 10-1/2p lower at 631-1/2p in heavy trading of over 22 million shares by late afternoon, having earlier slipped fractionally below six pounds.
The company had net funds of 1.05 billion pounds at the end of 1996, up 200 million pounds on 12 months earlier.
"We would like to return excess cash to shareholders," chief executive Peter Job said in an interview.
"We don't want to be pressed just because we have money to make acquisitions we don't really want," he added.
Job said he hoped other companies might now find a way to return cash to shareholders after the company's own plan to do so was "stamped on" by the British government last year.
Reuters was last October forced to abandon plans to return 613 million pounds to shareholders via a share buyback and special dividend after the government changed the tax rules for such schemes.
Asked about possible acquisitions, Job said Reuters did not really want to go outside its field of activity.
He said that reducing the number of competitors in its own competitive market would restrict clients' choice.
Job said he could not comment on reports linking Reuters with Dow Jones and Co Inc but noted they had been roundly denied by the other party.
He said that to gain critical mass Reuters had restructured its pricing to encourage conversions to its new 3000 range of products from the current 2000 series.
"This will make it difficult for the group to better the underlying revenue growth rate achieved in 1996," he said.
He said orders for the 3000 products, which combine real-time and historic data, were coming in faster than expected.

Job said that sales of 3000 products were ahead of expectations at a total of 14,700. He said installations stood at only 2,500 but added that this was an understandable result of the process of matching the product to clients' own systems.
Referring to the recent sharp appreciation in sterling, Job said, "...a robust sterling would severely restrict prospects for reported revenue and earnings growth."
However, he added, "..the strength of the underlying business is expected to enable Reuters to maintain double digit dividend growth in 1997."

Asked about the recent fall in the Reuters share price, Job said, "It does seem to me that the markets have a lot of sense behind them. Foreign exchange is a problem...If the pound continues very strong, it does reduce our rate of growth considerably, as we are saying."
The current share price compares with a high of over eight pounds reached last October.

The company also announced that GLOBEX, its automated matching system for futures contracts built with the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the MATIF futures exchange in France, was not likely to continue beyond 1998 as the original partners developed their own systems.
"This product has never been particularly successful and its closure will not produce any material impact on the company's results," Reuters said. ($1=.6120 Pound)
